title: Repeat it, or see it?
hookLine: two Advaita teachers argue over what repeating the saying does
carry: the great saying names what is, not a wish
tomorrow: a razor in its case, fire in a log. where's the self hiding?

lines: A LINE SAID TO A MIRROR.
cards: A mirror, first thing in the morning, and a line said to it: I am confident. I am enough. Again.
And again. Here's a fair question about the great saying, then. If someone says aham brahmasmi, I am Brahman, over and over, does it sink in until it's true for them?
Teachers inside Advaita itself argued about exactly this, and both sides had a strong case.

teach.h: MANDANA: A MAP, THEN THE WALK.
teach.b: One side is usually linked with Mandana Mishra, the same scholar the old story has debating Shankara under two garlands.
Hearing the saying, this view holds, gives a person knowledge, but at first it's secondhand, like a map of a city you've never walked.
To make it direct, a person meditates on it again and again, a long, steady practice, until the knowing becomes their own. The best case for it: that's how deep things are learned.
A musician hears a scale explained once and still practices for years. Shankara argued the other side. The saying isn't there to make anything so, he held.
It describes what already is. Something produced by practice would be new, and whatever is new can fade; the self the saying points to isn't produced at all.
It's like being told where your glasses are: once you look, saying it again adds nothing.
The best case for it: repetition can't make a truth truer. And Shankara didn't throw practice out.
Where understanding hasn't dawned yet, he allowed that hearing and reflecting may need to be repeated, to clear what's in the way.
Both sides honor the saying, and both keep the three steps the Brihadaranyaka itself names: hearing, reflecting, meditating; in Sanskrit, shravana, manana, nididhyasana.
They part over what the practice does: build the knowing, or clear the way for what was already there. Neither treats it as an affirmation. Aham brahmasmi names what is.

how: In Advaita study a student hears the great sayings from a teacher (shravana), reflects on them (manana), and meditates on them (nididhyasana); teachers in the tradition have long discussed how much that meditation does.

o: I am Brahman: the self is the one reality
I praise Brahman: a line of daily worship
I will be Brahman: a goal reached by effort

games.q: repeat it, or see it? tap the pairs.
p: the saying shows what already is
clears the way, adds no truth

s: aham brahmasmi works like an affirmation: say it enough and it comes true
neither side treats it as a slogan that makes itself true; they argue over how it becomes known.
Advaita teachers argued over whether hearing the saying is enough
one side held long meditation makes it direct; Shankara held the saying itself gives the knowledge.
Shankara rejected every kind of practice
he allowed that hearing and reflecting may need repeating where understanding hasn't dawned.

games.q: a friend sides with Shankara: 'hear it once, see it, done.' you're asked to give the other side's best case. what do you say?
o: deep things take practice: a musician hears a scale once and still practices for years.
the other side thinks the saying is false until you've said it enough times.
the other side thinks hearing scripture explained is useless.
games.why: the meditation view isn't that the saying is false; it's that knowledge first heard is secondhand, and long practice makes it direct.

practice: Write aham brahmasmi once, slowly, by hand. Then don't repeat it. Just look at the line for the rest of the sit, and let one question rest under the breath: is the I reading this something being built, or something already here?

wordCard.voice: Aham brahmasmi, and the argument inside Advaita about it: practiced until it's direct, or heard and seen, with practice clearing the way.

orig.note: Sanskrit aham brahmasmi, I am Brahman: the great saying of the Brihadaranyaka, argued over by its own readers.

carryVoice: Carry this: aham brahmasmi names what is, not a wish. On that much, both sides agree. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 4.1.1–2 (repetition of hearing and reflection for those in whom understanding has not arisen; for one in whom it arises, once suffices) and Upadeshasahasri, verse part, ch. 18 (against the view that repeated meditation, prasankhyana, is needed after hearing the saying)
Mandana Mishra, Brahmasiddhi (knowledge from the Upanishadic sentence made direct by repeated meditation, prasankhyana) (paraphrased framing)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (Yajnavalkya to Maitreyi: the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on), the root of the Advaita steps shravana, manana, nididhyasana
